amendments.rule: Prefer the smallest defensible semantic unit. Split only when every resulting correspondence is independently defensible and that source–target allocation is clearly preferable to materially plausible alternatives; an imaginable partition is not enough. Judge lexical and grammatical contributions in context: a correspondence need not be a dictionary-literal gloss or exclude ordinary English helpers. Where English expresses a construction jointly and its pieces cannot be assigned non-arbitrarily, retain the fused rendering as `noncompositional`. Source or target token count is diagnostic, never sufficient grounds to split. This tests ownership of the rendering, not alternative heads or helper placements already settled by a specific rule; explicit rulings below, including fused `aligned` renderings, retain precedence. **And because it tests ownership of a rendering, it does not reach English that no source morpheme owns.** A run of supplied English answering to no morpheme at all is one `added` unit where its words stand together and do one office in the clause, however many words it runs to and however many separate rules account for their absence from the source: rule 43 already places a supplied *have* together with any numeral, subject or object the ASV supplies alongside it, rule 20 a supplied lexical verb together with a supplied object, and rule 33 a supplied preposition together with the supplied noun it stands before. Head such a unit on the word carrying its force under rules 24 and 31, or leave the head null where no word carries it, which rule 5 permits. Do not divide it word by word on this rule's preference for the smallest unit: there is no source–target allocation to test between its parts, so nothing distinguishes them, and what the ledger asks is only that the whole run be partitioned once. Contiguity and office are the conditions, exactly as contiguity is in rules 30 and 55. Where the ASV's own rendered material stands between two runs of supplied English they are two units, each placed by the rule that governs it, as rule 20 makes the dummy and copula of a cleft one unit and the cleft relative standing beyond the predicate another; and where two adjacent supplied words do different offices — a noun supplied for a possessive to stand on beside a connective supplied for the next colon — they are two units on the same terms. `נָצְרוּ דָעַת` → *preserve* ***him that hath*** *knowledge* is one `added` unit headed on *hath*, and `טוֹב־עַיִן הוּא` → *He* ***that hath*** *a bountiful eye* is one likewise, a supplied relative and a supplied verb of having composing between them the single office of making the Hebrew predicate into a relative clause.
amendments.why: PRO.22 analysed one and the same supplied device two ways: 22.9 split 'that hath' into two `added` units citing this rule's smallest-unit preference, while 22.12 kept 'him that hath' as one. The sentence that misled it is this rule's own, so the qualification belongs here rather than in a new rule pointing back at it. The contract already bundles supplied English in three places (rules 20, 33, 43), and rule 20's cleft shows what the limit is: 'It is' and 'that' stand apart across the clause's rendered predicate and are two units. Contiguity and office are therefore written in as the condition, which leaves every existing ruling standing and settles the granularity question the ledger otherwise leaves open. The lemma table is keyed by source lemma and cannot see `added` units, so this class of split is only ever found by reading a chapter end to end.

conventions: Phrasal particles are kept with their verbs throughout this chapter, and rule 44's surplus-particle carve-out was considered and declined in each case: 'Train up' (22.6), 'bound up' (22.15), 'pass on' (22.3), 'Cast out' and 'go out' (22.10), 'carry back' (22.21), 'take away' (22.27). Where the bare English verb arguably writes the whole lexeme already -- 'up' on חָנַךְ and on קָשַׁר, 'away' on לָקַח -- the competing `added` reading is named in the verse's own note. A later verse in this chapter should fold the particle and name the alternative rather than mark it `added`.

Rule 30 fusions in this chapter are recorded with status `noncompositional` rather than `aligned`: עַל־פִּי (22.6), בְּבִטְנְ- (22.18), בַּחוּץ and בְּתוֹךְ (22.13), אִישׁ מַלְוֶה (22.7), לָמָּה (22.27), וְאַל (22.22) and both לִפְנֵי (22.29). The corpus records fused prepositions both ways -- לִפְנֵי is `aligned` to 'before' in 597 units and `noncompositional` in 269 -- so the choice is free and the chapter made it uniformly.

report: One real cross-verse split, and it is invisible to the lemma table because it lives entirely in `added` units. PRO.22.9 splits the supplied 'that hath' of 'He that hath a bountiful eye' into two `added` units; PRO.22.12 keeps the identical device -- a supplied relative plus a supplied verb of having, over a Hebrew that writes no possessive morpheme -- as the single unit 'him that hath'. Nothing in either source licenses the difference. PRO.22.9 is patched to the one-unit reading, headed on 'hath'.

Direction of the fix: rules 20, 33 and 43 each already bundle supplied English with whatever the ASV supplies alongside it, and rule 2 is written as a test of source-target allocation, which has no grip between two words that answer to no morpheme at all. PRO.22.9's own note cited rule 2 for the split and over-read it. The rest of the chapter already follows the merged practice: 22.3's 'for it' is one unit, and 22.16's adjacent 'gain' and 'And' are two only because they do two offices.

Not splits, checked and left standing. lamed before Ncmsa: 22.7's 'to the lender' is an adjunct dative in a clause whose predicate is עֶבֶד, while 22.16's lamed is itself the verbless clause's predicate and takes the result frame under rule 49. Article as 'the' (22.22), 'this' (22.19, rule 41) and unrepresented (22.6). Beth as 'in', 'of', 'over' and inside four fusions. אַל as 'no' in 22.24, where the ASV recasts the negation onto the nominal under rule 15, against 'not' in 22.22, 22.26 and 22.28. כִּי as 'For', 'because', 'when', 'if'. Every difference is read off the ASV.

22.1's three מִן against two written 'than's: two aligned to 'rather than' headed on 'than' (rule 24's twenty-five corpus units), the third unrepresented under rule 22 because the ASV writes one 'than' for 'silver and gold'. Correct as it stands.

BSB: all four disagreements (22.1 מִ, 22.6 לַ, 22.16 ל, 22.27 לְ) are prepositions the ASV's recasting leaves with no English word of their own, which rule 40 marks unrepresented and BSB attaches to its phrase. None is a genuine error, and no accepted edge was changed to move the rate.

Two chapter-wide judgments are logged that were reached in six and nine verses without being recorded: every phrasal particle is kept with its verb (rule 44's surplus-particle carve-out was considered and declined in each), and every rule-30 fusion is recorded `noncompositional` rather than `aligned`, which the corpus does both ways.

The added-unit finding is returned as an amendment to rule 2 rather than a new rule, so the sentence that misled this chapter is corrected where it stands. Contiguity and office are written in as its limit, so rule 20's cleft -- where 'It is' and 'that' stand apart across the predicate -- still splits into two units.
